provisions.heading: Definitions
provisions.text: “roadway” means the part of the highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, but does not include the shoulder, and, where a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term “roadway” refers to any one roadway separately and not to all of the roadways collectively;

provisions.heading: Definitions
provisions.text: “vehicle” includes a motor vehicle, trailer, traction engine, farm tractor, road-building machine, bicycle and any vehicle drawn, propelled or driven by any kind of power, including muscular power, but does not include a motorized snow vehicle or a street car;

provisions.heading: Left turn, across path of approaching vehicle
provisions.text: (5) No driver or operator of a vehicle in an intersection shall turn left across the path of a vehicle approaching from the opposite direction unless he or she has afforded a reasonable opportunity to the driver or operator of the approaching vehicle to avoid a collision.

provisions.heading: Signal when moving from parked position
provisions.text: (2) The driver or operator of a vehicle parked or stopped on the highway before setting the vehicle in motion shall first see that the movement can be made in safety, and, if in turning the vehicle the operation of any other vehicle may be affected by the movement, shall give a signal plainly visible to the driver or operator of the other vehicle of the intention to make the movement.

provisions.heading: Exception
provisions.text: (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to a driver of a, (a) vehicle while overtaking and passing another vehicle proceeding in the same direction; (b) vehicle while preparing for a left turn at an intersection or into a private road or driveway; (c) road service vehicle; or (d) bicycle in a lane designated under subsection 153 (2) for travel in the opposite direction of traffic.

provisions.heading: Passing meeting vehicles
provisions.text: 148 (1) Every person in charge of a vehicle on a highway meeting another vehicle shall turn out to the right from the centre of the roadway, allowing the other vehicle one-half of the roadway free.

provisions.heading: Vehicles or equestrians overtaking others
provisions.text: (5) Every person in charge of a vehicle or on horseback on a highway who is overtaking another vehicle or equestrian shall turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision with the vehicle or equestrian overtaken, and the person overtaken is not required to leave more than one-half of the roadway free.

provisions.heading: Bicycles overtaken
provisions.text: (6) Every person on a bicycle or motor assisted bicycle who is overtaken by a vehicle or equestrian travelling at a greater speed shall turn out to the right and allow the vehicle or equestrian to pass and the vehicle or equestrian overtaking shall turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision.

provisions.heading: Same
provisions.text: (3.1) If all or part of a bus operated under the authority of a permit issued under subsection 7 (7) is painted chrome yellow, the bus shall display, (a) on its front and rear the words “school bus”; and (b) on its rear, (i) the words “do not pass when signals flashing”, if the school bus was manufactured before January 1, 2005, or (ii) the words “do not pass when red lights flashing” if the school bus was manufactured on or after January 1, 2005.

provisions.heading: Overhead signal-lights
provisions.text: (4.1) Every school bus registered in Ontario that is manufactured on or after January 1, 2005 shall be equipped with four overhead red signal-lights and four overhead amber signal-lights mounted outside of the bus at or near the roof line in the following configuration: 1. One red signal-light and one amber signal-light on each side of the bus at the front. 2. One red signal-light and one amber signal-light on each side of the bus at the rear.

provisions.heading: Lamps required on all motor vehicles except motorcycles
provisions.text: 62 (1) When on a highway at any time from one-half hour before sunset to one-half hour after sunrise and at any other time when, due to insufficient light or unfavourable atmospheric conditions, persons and vehicles on the highway are not clearly discernible at a distance of 150 metres or less, every motor vehicle other than a motorcycle shall carry three lighted lamps in a conspicuous position, one on each side of the front of the vehicle which shall display a white or amber light only, and one on the rear of the vehicle which shall display a red light only.

provisions.heading: Definition, “race” and “contest”
provisions.text: 2. (1) For the purposes of section 172 of the Act, “race” and “contest” include any activity where one or more persons engage in any of the following driving behaviours: 1. Driving two or more motor vehicles at a rate of speed that is a marked departure from the lawful rate of speed and in a manner that indicates the drivers of the motor vehicles are engaged in a competition.

(2) Subsection (1) does not apply to a person operating a commercial motor vehicle if, (a) the vehicle is a bus, an ambulance or a fire apparatus; (b) the vehicle is engaged in maintenance or construction; (c) the vehicle is a tow truck that has been requested to provide towing services or roadside assistance services to a vehicle in or near the left lane, and operating the tow truck in the lane is necessary to access the location of the vehicle; or (d) an emergency requires the use of the lane by the vehicle.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p10a|J|too narrow to be shared safely

handbook.says: The handbook gives no lane width: it says only that drivers passing a cyclist 'must maintain a minimum distance of one metre, where practical' and that two-wheelers riding to one side are not 'an invitation to pass in the same lane' but should be passed 'by changing lanes', which bears on when a lane is too narrow to share without measuring it.

law.says: The Act gives no lane width either: 147 (1) keeps a slower vehicle to the right 'where practicable' and 'as close as practicable' to the edge, and 148 (6.1) asks a passing motorist to leave one metre 'as nearly as may be practicable'.

flags.note: Reading 'too narrow' as a lane in which a motor vehicle cannot pass the cyclist while leaving one metre would combine 148 (6.1) with the width of the vehicle; no source says so, so it is not counted.

handbook.says: The list under this lead names other cases ('Avoid obstacles such as puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates'; 'Cross railway or streetcar tracks at a 90° angle') and the passing chapter adds 'to avoid dangerous road conditions or to be seen by other drivers', but for discouraging passing the only test is the lane being too narrow to share, which is itself unmeasured.

law.says: 147 (1) keeps a slower vehicle to the right only 'where practicable' and gives no test of when leaving the edge is needed for safety.

flags.note: The handbook lists discouraging passing in a too-narrow lane as one of its 'necessary for safety' cases, so in p10a this condition adds nothing beyond the 'too narrow to be shared safely' flag, which is also open. (mto:3.4.4a, which is not limited to discouraging passing, is PARTIAL.)

handbook.says: The only neighbouring guidance is equally open, 'Whenever possible, you should change lanes to pass'; the handbook never says when one metre is not practical.

law.says: 148 (6.1) asks for the one metre 'as nearly as may be practicable' with no test of when less is allowed; 148 (6.2) only says how the metre is measured ('the extreme right side of the motor vehicle and the extreme left side of the bicycle, including all projections and attachments'), and demerit item 44 gives 2 points.

flags.note: 148 (6.2) could be added to say how the 1 m is measured, but it does not settle 'where practical'; the Act does not define 'practicable'.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook drops the qualifier ('Do not take this as an invitation to pass in the same lane'; 'If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes'), but no sentence says when a lane change to pass a cyclist is possible.

law.says: 148 (6) asks the overtaking vehicle to 'turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision' and 148 (6.1) sets the one-metre minimum; neither requires or tests a lane change.

flags.definition: Letting the faster vehicle pass in safety means moving to the right (closer to the right side of the lane on an undivided road), not speeding up, and being ready to slow down so it can get in front sooner.

flags.definition: For a lane change, including a pass on a multi-lane road: at least a two- to three-second gap behind the vehicle ahead in the new lane, without moving in beside another vehicle or into its blind spot.
flags.effect: Could replace 'enough space' for lane changes; no measure for a pass on a two-lane road.
flags.note: The mirror test for moving back after a pass (changing-positions:029.1) marks when the pass is complete, not the room it needs.

handbook.says: For lane changes only, the road test's lane-change task spells out the safe move: 'at least a two- to three-second distance behind the vehicle in front of you', not moving 'in beside another vehicle or into the blind spot of another vehicle', and 'Adjust your speed to match the speed of traffic in the new lane'; nothing like it is given for a pass on a two-lane road.

law.says: The Act uses the same words with no measure: 'in safety' (142 (1)), 'safely' (154 (1) (a)) and 'safely free' (148 (8)).

flags.definition: For a lane change: at least a two- to three-second gap behind the vehicle ahead in the new lane, not beside another vehicle or in its blind spot, at the speed of traffic in the new lane.
flags.effect: Could replace 'safely' with these checks for lane changes; a pass on a two-lane road stays open.

handbook.says: The neighbours stay open: 'If in doubt, do not pass', and the passing steps ask the driver to 'check that the way is clear ahead and behind' and to watch for bicycles and small vehicles 'that may be hidden from view', without a test of certainty.

law.says: The Act puts the same judgment on the driver: first ascertain 'that it can be done safely' (154 (1) (a)), 'first see that the movement can be made in safety' (142 (1)), and a roadway 'safely free from approaching traffic' (148 (8)).

flags.effect: Strength: 148 (8) makes it a duty for every pass, and 154 (1) (a) for any pass that moves from one lane to another.

handbook.says: The handbook uses doubt the same open way elsewhere ('If you're in doubt, let the other driver go first') and frames a pass as needing the driver to be 'sure you can do so without danger to yourself or others', with no test of doubt.

law.says: 154 (1) (a) allows a lane-to-lane move only if the driver first ascertains 'that it can be done safely' and 148 (8) requires a roadway 'safely free from approaching traffic', so a driver in doubt has not met them, but the Act neither names nor tests the state.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook stays open: where 'you cannot see far ahead on the road because of a curve or a hill, move right', and a pass is made only 'if there are enough broken lines ahead to complete the pass safely'; no clear distance is given.

law.says: 149 (1) (a) forbids driving left of centre 'when approaching the crest of a grade or upon a curve in the roadway' where the view is obstructed 'so as to create a potential hazard', and 148 (8) asks for a roadway 'safely free from approaching traffic', with no clear distance.

flags.effect: Strength: 149 (1) (a) makes it a prohibition on roads with one or more lanes each way (3 demerit points, item 12).
flags.note: Whether the 30 metres of 149 (1) (a) also limits the crest and curve cases is unclear from its wording and is not counted. An engineering passing sight distance (OTM Book 11) was not obtained.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook stays open: where 'you cannot see far ahead on the road because of a curve or a hill, move right', and a pass is made only 'if there are enough broken lines ahead to complete the pass safely'; no clear distance is given.

law.says: 149 (1) (a) forbids driving left of centre 'when approaching the crest of a grade or upon a curve in the roadway' where the view is obstructed 'so as to create a potential hazard', and 148 (8) asks for a roadway 'safely free from approaching traffic', with no clear distance.

flags.note: Whether the 30 metres of 149 (1) (a) also limits the crest and curve cases is unclear from its wording and is not counted. An engineering passing sight distance (OTM Book 11) was not obtained.

handbook.says: The next sentences say which marking tells it: 'A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass', while 'A broken line at the left of your lane means you may pass if the way is clear'.

law.says: The Act and regulations given do not give pavement lines a meaning.

flags.definition: The markings tell it by a solid line at the left of the driver's lane: passing is not safe there; a broken line allows a pass if the way is clear.
flags.effect: Could name the marking: a solid line at the left of the lane.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook stays open: 'be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely' and 'check that the way is clear ahead and behind'; no length of broken line or passing distance is given.

law.says: 148 (8) asks that the roadway ahead and to the left be 'safely free from approaching traffic', with no distance; the Act and regulations given do not mention broken lines.

flags.note: The mirror test (changing-positions:029.1) marks where a pass ends but not how far ahead the broken line must run. An engineering passing sight distance (OTM Book 11) was not obtained.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook stays open: 'be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely' and 'check that the way is clear ahead and behind'; no length of broken line or passing distance is given.

law.says: 148 (8) asks that the roadway ahead and to the left be 'safely free from approaching traffic', with no distance; the Act and regulations given do not mention broken lines.

handbook.says: No other sentence says what makes a pass in the left lane of a passing or climbing lane safe.

law.says: The Act and regulations given do not define passing or climbing lanes.

flags.note: Inside a definition, about the lane's purpose; it sets no duty. The sign 'Keep to the right lane except when passing on two-lane sections where climbing or passing lanes are provided' (signs:071.1) restates the use, and 149 (2) (a) lifts the crest and curve ban where one direction has more lanes, but neither defines 'safely'.

handbook.says: The merge is a lane change, for which the road test measures the space: 'at least a two- to three-second distance behind the vehicle in front of you', without moving 'in beside another vehicle or into the blind spot of another vehicle'; traffic coming from behind in the left lane is not measured.

law.says: 154 (1) (a) allows a move from one lane to another only if the driver first ascertains 'that it can be done safely', with no measure.

flags.definition: Merge with at least a two- to three-second gap behind the vehicle ahead in the left lane, without moving in beside another vehicle or into its blind spot.
flags.effect: Could add the gap and side checks; the gap to traffic behind stays open.

handbook.says: For some cases: 'Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle', 'Traffic should keep to the right, using the left lanes for passing', and freeway drivers 'should move over, if it is safe to do so, leaving room for merging vehicles'; other reasons the right lane cannot be used are not named.

law.says: For slower vehicles only: 147 (1) requires the right-hand lane 'where practicable', and 147 (2) lifts this 'while overtaking and passing another vehicle' or 'while preparing for a left turn'; nothing applies to traffic at the normal speed and 'practicable' is not tested.

flags.definition: Drive in the right-hand lane except while passing, preparing to turn left, or moving over to leave room for merging traffic; other cases where the right lane cannot be used stay open.
flags.effect: Could replace 'when possible' with the named exceptions.

handbook.says: For some cases: the list names 'Avoid obstacles such as puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates' and 'Cross railway or streetcar tracks at a 90° angle', and the passing chapter adds 'to avoid dangerous road conditions or to be seen by other drivers'; the list is open ('such as').

law.says: 147 (1) keeps a slower vehicle to the right only 'where practicable', with no test.

flags.definition: Necessary for safety covers at least: avoiding obstacles such as puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates; crossing railway or streetcar tracks at a right angle; being seen by other drivers; and discouraging passing where the lane is too narrow to share (itself unmeasured). Other cases stay open.
flags.effect: Could list the named cases.
flags.note: Cyclists at or above the normal speed of traffic, or turning left, need not keep right at all (sharing-road-other-road-users:028.1; 147 (1) applies only to slower vehicles and 147 (2) (b) exempts preparing for a left turn).

handbook.says: The handbook gives no lane width: it says only that drivers passing a cyclist 'must maintain a minimum distance of one metre, where practical' and that two-wheelers riding to one side are not 'an invitation to pass in the same lane' but should be passed 'by changing lanes', which bears on when a lane is too narrow to share without measuring it.

law.says: The Act gives no lane width either: 147 (1) keeps a slower vehicle to the right 'where practicable' and 'as close as practicable' to the edge, and 148 (6.1) asks a passing motorist to leave one metre 'as nearly as may be practicable'.

flags.note: Reading 'too narrow' as a lane in which a motor vehicle cannot pass the cyclist while leaving one metre would combine 148 (6.1) with the width of the vehicle; no source says so, so it is not counted.

handbook.says: The only neighbouring guidance is equally open, 'Whenever possible, you should change lanes to pass'; the handbook never says when one metre is not practical.

law.says: 148 (6.1) asks for the one metre 'as nearly as may be practicable' with no test of when less is allowed; 148 (6.2) only says how the metre is measured ('the extreme right side of the motor vehicle and the extreme left side of the bicycle, including all projections and attachments'), and demerit item 44 gives 2 points.

flags.note: 148 (6.2) could be added to say how the 1 m is measured, but it does not settle 'where practical'; the Act does not define 'practicable'.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook drops the qualifier ('Do not take this as an invitation to pass in the same lane'; 'If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes'), but no sentence says when a lane change to pass a cyclist is possible.

law.says: 148 (6) asks the overtaking vehicle to 'turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision' and 148 (6.1) sets the one-metre minimum; neither requires or tests a lane change.

flags.note: On a two-lane road a lane change to pass means using the opposing lane, so the passing limits (solid line at the left, 30 m of a crossover, 148 (8)) would bear on 'possible', but none is tied to this rule. The unqualified wording of changing-positions:022.3 differs from 'whenever possible'.

handbook.says: The neighbours stay open: large commercial vehicles 'require a much longer distance to stop than smaller vehicles', and the stopping-distance figure compares a tractor-trailer with a much smaller vehicle without a number.

law.says: The Act says nothing about the room a large vehicle needs to stop.

flags.note: The handbook's mirror test for moving back after a pass ('when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror', changing-positions:017.2, 029.1) bears on the separate 'closely' flag, not on the stopping cushion, and for large vehicles the handbook asks for more room than that. The move back into the lane falls under 154 (1) (a), whose 'can be done safely' is equally open.

handbook.says: For some cases only: 'A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass'; nothing says when passing a slow vehicle is safe.

law.says: 148 (8) allows a pass only where the roadway ahead and to the left is 'safely free from approaching traffic' and to the left 'safely free from overtaking traffic', with no distance.

flags.definition: Not safe at least where there is a solid line at the left of the driver's lane; on other roads it stays the driver's judgment.
flags.effect: Could add the solid-line case; the judgment stays open elsewhere.
flags.note: Where passing is not permitted at all (within 30 m of a pedestrian crossover, left of centre within 30 m of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel: changing-positions:020.1, 020.2; 140 (3), 149 (1)) the result is the same. An engineering passing sight distance (OTM Book 11) was not obtained.

handbook.says: For the following distance: 'A safe following distance is at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front of you', a minimum that 'applies only to ideal driving conditions'; for the pass, only some cases: 'A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass'.

law.says: 158 (1) forbids following 'more closely than is reasonable and prudent' and 148 (8) asks for a roadway 'safely free from approaching traffic', neither with a measure.

flags.definition: Following distance: at least two seconds behind the horse-drawn vehicle in ideal conditions, more in bad weather; passing is not safe at least where a solid line is at the left of the lane.
flags.effect: Could use two seconds for the following distance; passing stays open beyond the solid-line case.
flags.note: (Pass part same as on-passing-1:p17a.)

handbook.says: No other sentence gives a passing distance for horse-drawn vehicles; the one-metre rule is for cyclists.

law.says: 148 (5) asks the overtaking driver to 'turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision', equally open; the one-metre rule of 148 (6.1) is for bicycles only.

flags.note: A horse-drawn vehicle is a 'vehicle' under s. 1 (1) of the Act (vehicles drawn by muscular power), so 148 (5) applies.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook says 'Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions' and that a plow wing 'extends as far as three metres to the right of the vehicle', so no room between plows is treated as enough; it gives no clearance figure.

law.says: 148.1 (1) forbids overtaking a plow 'travelling in echelon with another plow or plows' on a highway posted 80 km/h or more with two or more marked lanes in the driver's direction 'unless the lane of travel that is used by the overtaking vehicle to overtake the snow plow is entirely clear of any part of the snow plow, including any part of an attachment or the plow blade'.

flags.definition: Room is enough only if the lane used to overtake is entirely clear of any part of the plows, including attachments and blades; with plows staggered across all lanes no lane is, and the handbook says not to pass moving plows at all.
flags.effect: Strength LAW on highways posted 80 km/h or more with two or more lanes in the driver's direction, with the Act's test in place of 'enough room'.
flags.note: The handbook (never pass a moving plow) is stricter than the Act (allowed when the lane is entirely clear); a freeway posted below 80 km/h would fall outside 148.1 but inside the handbook's ban.

handbook.says: In part: the move-over steps ask the driver to 'double check your rearview mirrors and shoulder check your blind spots to ensure no other vehicles are moving into or approaching that lane too fast', and the lane-change task measures the space as 'at least a two- to three-second distance behind the vehicle in front of you', without moving 'in beside another vehicle or into the blind spot of another vehicle'; traffic coming from behind is left at 'too fast'.

law.says: 159 (3) (and its version in force January 1, 2027) requires the move into another lane 'if the movement can be made safely', and demerit item 36.3 reads 'if safe to do so', with no measure.

flags.definition: Safe to move over at least requires a two- to three-second gap behind the vehicle ahead in the new lane and not moving in beside another vehicle or into its blind spot; the gap to traffic approaching from behind stays a judgment.
flags.effect: Could add the gap and side checks; the Act's test stays 'can be made safely'.
flags.note: The handbook's demerit list says 'where possible' (keeping-your-drivers-licence:106.1, a source here), which differs from 'if safe to do so' in 097.1 and in item 36.3.

handbook.says: Outside the towing paragraph the handbook only repeats 'be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely'; the towing paragraph itself asks for more space with no figure.

law.says: 148 (8) asks that the roadway be 'safely free' of approaching and overtaking traffic, with no distance and nothing for trailers.

flags.note: The road test's two- to three-second lane-change gap and the mirror test are for ordinary vehicles; the towing section says a trailer needs more, so they do not settle it.

handbook.says: The handbook spells out what the driver being passed does: 'do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you. It is unlawful and dangerous', on an undivided road 'move closer to the right side of the lane', and 'Be prepared to slow down to let the passing driver get in front of you more quickly'.

law.says: 148 (2) requires a driver who is overtaken to 'turn out to the right and allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass' with no safety qualifier (fine under 148 (2.1)), and the stunt regulation lists driving 'in a manner that indicates an intention to prevent another vehicle from passing'.

flags.definition: Letting the faster vehicle pass in safety means moving to the right (closer to the right side of the lane on an undivided road), not speeding up, and being ready to slow down so it can get in front sooner.
flags.effect: Could replace 'in safety' with these actions; strength LAW under 148 (2).
flags.note: The Act's duty has no 'in safety' qualifier.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook leaves the need to the driver's own judgment: "If you need to get another person's attention, use your horn", "Avoid honking your horn at other drivers, unless absolutely necessary", and the next sentence "If you feel that you must use your horn, tap it quickly and lightly"; none says when the horn is necessary.

law.says: Section 75(4) bars sounding a horn "so as to make an unreasonable noise" and 75(5) requires it to be sounded "whenever it is reasonably necessary to notify pedestrians or others of its approach"; both leave necessity to a reasonableness judgment with no test.

flags.note: The purpose is narrowed (to get attention, or to warn of approach) but not when that is needed. The handbook makes it the driver's call ("if you feel that you must"), while the Act's "reasonably necessary" is an objective standard.

handbook.says: No other sentence of the handbook gives a distance, or any other measure, for when to sound the horn while coming up on a cyclist.

law.says: Section 75(5) requires the horn to be sounded "whenever it is reasonably necessary to notify pedestrians or others of its approach", which implies sounding it before reaching the cyclist but sets no distance.

flags.note: The one metre of 148(6.1) and the handbook's "minimum distance of one metre" is side clearance while passing, not a horn distance, so it is not counted; the only handbook guide is the purpose in the preceding sentence (the horn "may frighten them").

handbook.says: For only a minimum: the general passing steps say to move back "when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror", at which point "you are far enough ahead to pull back", but for large vehicles the same paragraph adds that they "require a much longer distance to stop" and asks drivers to "allow more room", without saying how much more than that test.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: At the least, do not move back in front of the large vehicle until its entire front is visible in the inside (rear-view) mirror; the extra room a large vehicle needs beyond that is not measured.
flags.effect: Could cite the mirror test of the passing steps as the minimum in place of "closely", leaving the large-vehicle margin as advice.
flags.note: The earlier pass treated the mirror test as resolving this; it is a general test for any vehicle, and the handbook's own "allow more room" and the longer stopping distance of large vehicles make it a floor only. The two-second rule is the follower's own gap and is not counted.

handbook.says: For only the baseline: after any pass "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back", and large vehicles "require a much longer distance to stop" and need a "space cushion", but the handbook never says how much more room than that baseline to allow.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: More than the general minimum: stay out of the lane in front of the large vehicle at least until its whole front shows in the inside mirror, and then longer; the size of the extra margin is not given.
flags.effect: Could state the mirror test as the minimum and keep "more room" as advice for the extra margin.
flags.note: Read in its paragraph (under "Stopping Distance"), "more room" is the gap left ahead of the large vehicle when moving back; the turbulence item ("may affect your ability to control your vehicle when passing a large one", 057.3) could also suggest side room, which no source measures.

handbook.says: For only a minimum: "A safe following distance is at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front of you" (counted against a fixed marker; reaching it sooner means "you are following too closely"), the road test asks for "at least a two- to three-second distance", and the handbook calls this "a minimum following distance" that needs "extra space in certain situations"; it gives no measure for "well back" beyond that.

law.says: Section 158(1) bars following "more closely than is reasonable and prudent having due regard for the speed of the vehicle and the traffic on and the conditions of the highway", with no distance.

flags.definition: At least the two-second following distance (two to three seconds on the road test) behind the farm machinery; how much farther "well back" asks for is not said.
flags.effect: Could replace "well back" with "at least two seconds behind", noting that more is advised.
flags.note: Farm machinery is not among the situations listed for extra space (bad weather, motorcycles, large trucks, heavy loads), though the handbook notes it is often oversized and its driver may not see vehicles coming up behind (068.3); "well back" suggests more than the minimum.

handbook.says: The neighbouring sentences ask only to "give as much distance between you and them as possible" when passing and, for a buggy coming the other way, to "move to the far right of your lane"; no distance is given.

law.says: Section 148(5) requires a driver overtaking another vehicle or equestrian to "turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision", which is equally open; the one-metre rule of 148(6.1) applies only to bicycles.

flags.note: The one-metre figure (148(6.1); handbook "minimum distance of one metre") is for cyclists and is not counted for horse-drawn vehicles.

handbook.says: No handbook sentence gives the amount of the fine for failing to stop for a school bus.

law.says: Section 175(17) sets the fine for contravening 175(11) or (12) at not less than $400 and not more than $2,000 for a first offence, and $1,000 to $4,000 or up to six months' imprisonment, or both, for each subsequent offence; O. Reg. 339/94, item 14, gives 6 demerit points.

flags.definition: A fine of $400 to $2,000 for a first offence (175(17)(a)); $1,000 to $4,000, or up to six months in jail, or both, for a subsequent offence (175(17)(b)); plus 6 demerit points (O. Reg. 339/94, item 14).
flags.effect: Replace "a heavy fine" with "a fine of $400 to $2,000" for a first offence.
flags.note: The handbook's offence table lists "Failing to stop for a school bus" under six points (keeping-your-drivers-licence:084.1), matching item 14.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook says to "look well ahead and watch for people in parked vehicles, they may be about to pull out in front of you or to open a door", and on the road test to keep "away from parked vehicles" where there are no lane markings; it sets no standard for how closely to watch.

law.says: The Act sets no watching duty for the passing driver; the door duty in 165(1) falls on the person who opens the door.

law.says: Section 148(2) makes turning out to the right for a faster overtaking vehicle a duty but sets no time, and 154(1)(a) allows the lane change only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely".

flags.definition: At the first gap in the right-hand lane that lets the driver keep at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead without moving in beside another vehicle or into its blind spot.
flags.effect: Could replace "as soon as you can" with "at the first gap that meets the lane-change test".
flags.note: The gap behind ("no one is coming too fast from behind") and how long the driver may wait for a gap are not measured.

handbook.says: For some steps: the sentences after it say "Switch your headlights to low beams as you approach a vehicle from behind", "As you move alongside the vehicle you are passing, switch on your high beams", and move back "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror", with low beams "when you are less than 60 metres behind another vehicle unless you are passing it"; the hazard is that "you cannot see as far ahead, even with headlights", and nothing else is measured.

law.says: For headlight use only: section 168 requires the low beam when approaching an oncoming vehicle within 150 metres and when following another vehicle within 60 metres, "except when in the act of overtaking and passing".

flags.definition: Use low beams while within 60 metres behind the vehicle (and within 150 metres of oncoming traffic), switch to high beams once alongside, and move back only when the whole front of the passed vehicle shows in the rear-view mirror; nothing measures the rest of "very careful".
flags.effect: Could replace "be very careful" with the listed night steps, keeping the caution as advice.
flags.note: The earlier pass found no night standard; the steps right after the sentence supply one in part, and 168 matches the beam steps.

handbook.says: The other statement of this rule says the same: "Pass these safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed" and "Always be ready, in case pedestrians make sudden or unexpected moves"; no speed is given.

law.says: Section 166(1) lifts the two-metre rule where a safety zone has been designated and says nothing about the speed for passing it.

flags.note: The posted speed limit caps the speed but is not a measure of "reasonable", so it is not counted.

handbook.says: The next sentence adds one concrete step, "If safe to do so, move over a lane to increase the space between your vehicle and the hazard", and for construction zones the handbook says "drive carefully and adjust your driving to suit the conditions"; neither measures caution.

law.says: No provision in force covers these workers and vehicles; from January 1, 2027, 159(2) adds a stopped "work-related vehicle" with amber flashing lamps and asks the driver to "slow down and proceed with caution, having due regard for traffic on and the conditions of the highway and the weather", the same open word.

flags.note: Which vehicles count as work-related is left to a regulation under 159(12) (in force 2027), which is not among the sources; a roadside assistance vehicle that is a tow truck with amber flashing lamps is already covered by 159(2).

handbook.says: The next sentences say what to do while slowing, "assess the speed of the surrounding traffic and the condition of the roadway" and "brake early and gradually", and the offence table says "carefully pass"; no measure of caution or speed is given.

law.says: Section 159(2) uses the same words, "slow down and proceed with caution", adding only the factors ("having due regard for traffic on and the conditions of the highway and the weather") and the goal ("to ensure that the driver does not collide with the emergency vehicle or tow truck or endanger any person outside"); the 2027 version keeps them and the demerit item repeats "proceed with caution".

flags.note: The Act's goal (no collision, no danger to anyone outside the stopped vehicle) could be added after "caution" to say what it is for, but it is not a measure, so the earlier definition is moved here.

handbook.says: The handbook uses equally open words elsewhere, "be aware of any vehicles approaching fast to the rear of your vehicle" and, in the lane-change steps, "no one is coming too fast from behind or from two lanes over"; no speed is given.

law.says: Section 159(3) requires the move into another lane only "if the movement can be made safely", and 154(1)(a) only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely"; no speed is given for traffic coming up in the other lane.

law.says: Section 159(1) does not use "caution": it requires the driver to "immediately bring such vehicle to a standstill" as near as practicable to the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway (the nearest curb or edge on a one-way road of more than two lanes), parallel to it and clear of any intersection; the 2027 version keeps this, and item 35 gives 3 demerit points.

flags.effect: Replace "proceed with caution, clear the way and stop where required" in the legal part with the 159(1) standstill, and keep caution as advice.

law.says: Section 147(1) applies to "any vehicle travelling upon a roadway at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place" and requires it, "where practicable", to be driven in the right-hand lane then available or as close as practicable to the right curb or edge.

flags.definition: A vehicle travelling at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place (147(1)).
flags.effect: Replace "slow traffic" with this, and add the Act's "where practicable".
flags.note: 147(3) makes it an offence (fine $150 to $1,000).

handbook.says: For only the baseline: with a trailer "you also need more space because the length of your vehicle is much longer with a trailer attached", and after an ordinary pass "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back"; how much more room a trailer needs beyond that is not said.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: More than the ordinary point for moving back (the whole front of the passed vehicle showing in the mirror), because of the trailer's extra length; no amount is given.
flags.effect: Could state the mirror test as the minimum and keep "more room" for the trailer margin.
flags.note: A trailer may block the inside mirror; the handbook requires "additional mirrors that provide a clear view of the road to the rear" when the load blocks the view (towing:017.1), so the mirror test can still be applied.

handbook.says: For only a minimum: the ordinary point for moving back is "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back", and the sentences before ask a driver towing to "allow more room before you move back to your lane" because "the length of your vehicle is much longer with a trailer attached"; no later point is given.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: Moving back before the whole front of the passed vehicle shows in the mirror is too soon in every case; with a trailer the driver should wait longer, by an amount no source gives.
flags.effect: Could cite the mirror test as the earliest point and keep "too soon" for the trailer margin.
flags.note: The earlier note that a trailer may block the inside mirror is met by towing:017.1, which requires additional mirrors in that case.

law.says: No provision speaks to how to steer a trailer pushed aside by wind.

handbook.says: No other sentence gives an amount for the increase in speed.

law.says: No provision speaks to it; the speed limit caps any increase but does not measure "slight".

handbook.says: For some steps: the sentences after it say "Switch your headlights to low beams as you approach a vehicle from behind", "As you move alongside the vehicle you are passing, switch on your high beams", and move back "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror", with low beams "when you are less than 60 metres behind another vehicle unless you are passing it"; the hazard is that "you cannot see as far ahead, even with headlights", and nothing else is measured.

law.says: For headlight use only: section 168 requires the low beam when approaching an oncoming vehicle within 150 metres and when following another vehicle within 60 metres, "except when in the act of overtaking and passing".

flags.definition: Use low beams while within 60 metres behind the vehicle (and within 150 metres of oncoming traffic), switch to high beams once alongside, and move back only when the whole front of the passed vehicle shows in the rear-view mirror; nothing measures the rest of "very careful".
flags.effect: Could replace "be very careful" with the listed night steps, keeping the caution as advice.
flags.note: The earlier pass found no night standard; the steps right after the sentence supply one in part, and 168 matches the beam steps.

handbook.says: For a check after the fact: the road test says "You have not properly checked traffic if another vehicle or pedestrian has the right-of-way and must take action to avoid your vehicle", and the left-turn rules say to turn "after yielding the right-of-way to pedestrians and oncoming traffic" and not to "pull up beside it to make your turn at the same time"; no gap or time for starting is given.

law.says: Section 142(1) requires the driver to "first see that the movement can be made in safety", and 141(5) forbids turning left across an approaching vehicle's path unless the driver "has afforded a reasonable opportunity to the driver or operator of the approaching vehicle to avoid a collision"; neither sets a gap.

flags.definition: The way is not clear if any road user with the right-of-way (the smaller vehicle ahead, oncoming traffic or pedestrians) would have to take action to avoid your vehicle.
flags.effect: Could replace "clear" with the road test's check.
flags.note: The road test check says when a turn was wrong, after the fact; it gives no gap or time for deciding to start.

handbook.says: Elsewhere the handbook leaves the need to the driver's own judgment: "If you need to get another person's attention, use your horn", "Avoid honking your horn at other drivers, unless absolutely necessary", and the next sentence "If you feel that you must use your horn, tap it quickly and lightly"; none says when the horn is necessary.

law.says: Section 75(4) bars sounding a horn "so as to make an unreasonable noise" and 75(5) requires it to be sounded "whenever it is reasonably necessary to notify pedestrians or others of its approach"; both leave necessity to a reasonableness judgment with no test.

flags.note: On who judges: the next handbook sentence leaves it to the driver ("If you feel that you must use your horn"), while the Act's "unreasonable noise" and "reasonably necessary" are objective standards; the word itself still has no test.

handbook.says: No other sentence of the handbook gives a distance, or any other measure, for when to sound the horn while coming up on a cyclist.

law.says: Section 75(5) requires the horn to be sounded "whenever it is reasonably necessary to notify pedestrians or others of its approach", which implies sounding it before reaching the cyclist but sets no distance.

flags.note: The one metre of 148(6.1) and the handbook's "minimum distance of one metre" is side clearance while passing, not a horn distance, so it is not counted; the only handbook guide is the purpose in the same passage (the horn "may frighten them").

handbook.says: The other statement of this rule says the same: "Pass these safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed" and "Always be ready, in case pedestrians make sudden or unexpected moves"; no speed is given.

law.says: Section 166(1) lifts the two-metre rule where a safety zone has been designated and says nothing about the speed for passing it.

flags.note: The posted speed limit caps the speed but is not a measure of "reasonable", so it is not counted.

handbook.says: For only a minimum: the general passing steps say to move back "when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror", at which point "you are far enough ahead to pull back", but for large vehicles the same paragraph adds that they "require a much longer distance to stop" and asks drivers to "allow more room", without saying how much more than that test.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: At the least, do not move back in front of the large vehicle until its entire front is visible in the inside (rear-view) mirror; the extra room a large vehicle needs beyond that is not measured.
flags.effect: Could cite the mirror test of the passing steps as the minimum in place of "closely", leaving the large-vehicle margin as advice.
flags.note: The earlier pass treated the mirror test as resolving this; it is a general test for any vehicle, and the handbook's own "allow more room" and the longer stopping distance of large vehicles make it a floor only. The two-second rule is the follower's own gap and is not counted.

handbook.says: For only the baseline: after any pass "when you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back", and large vehicles "require a much longer distance to stop" and need a "space cushion", but the handbook never says how much more room than that baseline to allow.

law.says: The Act lets a driver move from one lane to another only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely" (154(1)(a)) or "first see[s] that the movement can be made in safety" (142(1)), and gives no distance or time.

flags.definition: More than the general minimum: stay out of the lane in front of the large vehicle at least until its whole front shows in the inside mirror, and then longer; the size of the extra margin is not given.
flags.effect: Could state the mirror test as the minimum and keep "more room" as advice for the extra margin.
flags.note: Read in its paragraph (under "Stopping Distance"), "more room" is the gap left ahead of the large vehicle when moving back; the turbulence item ("may affect your ability to control your vehicle when passing a large one", 057.3) could also suggest side room, which no source measures.

handbook.says: For only a minimum: "A safe following distance is at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front of you" (counted against a fixed marker; reaching it sooner means "you are following too closely"), the road test asks for "at least a two- to three-second distance", and the handbook calls this "a minimum following distance" that needs "extra space in certain situations"; it gives no measure for "well back" beyond that.

law.says: Section 158(1) bars following "more closely than is reasonable and prudent having due regard for the speed of the vehicle and the traffic on and the conditions of the highway", with no distance.

flags.definition: At least the two-second following distance (two to three seconds on the road test) behind the farm machinery; how much farther "well back" asks for is not said.
flags.effect: Could replace "well back" with "at least two seconds behind", noting that more is advised.
flags.note: Farm machinery is not among the situations listed for extra space (bad weather, motorcycles, large trucks, heavy loads), though the handbook notes it is often oversized and its driver may not see vehicles coming up behind (068.3); "well back" suggests more than the minimum.

handbook.says: No handbook sentence gives the amount of the fine for failing to stop for a school bus.

law.says: Section 175(17) sets the fine for contravening 175(11) or (12) at not less than $400 and not more than $2,000 for a first offence, and $1,000 to $4,000 or up to six months' imprisonment, or both, for each subsequent offence; O. Reg. 339/94, item 14, gives 6 demerit points.

flags.definition: A fine of $400 to $2,000 for a first offence (175(17)(a)); $1,000 to $4,000, or up to six months in jail, or both, for a subsequent offence (175(17)(b)); plus 6 demerit points (O. Reg. 339/94, item 14).
flags.effect: Replace "a heavy fine" with "a fine of $400 to $2,000" for a first offence.
flags.note: The handbook's offence table lists "Failing to stop for a school bus" under six points (keeping-your-drivers-licence:084.1), matching item 14.

handbook.says: The next sentences say what to do while slowing, "assess the speed of the surrounding traffic and the condition of the roadway" and "brake early and gradually", and the offence table says "carefully pass"; no measure of caution or speed is given.

law.says: Section 159(2) uses the same words, "slow down and proceed with caution", adding only the factors ("having due regard for traffic on and the conditions of the highway and the weather") and the goal ("to ensure that the driver does not collide with the emergency vehicle or tow truck or endanger any person outside"); the 2027 version keeps them and the demerit item repeats "proceed with caution".

flags.note: The Act's goal (no collision, no danger to anyone outside the stopped vehicle) could be added after "caution" to say what it is for, but it is not a measure, so the earlier definition is moved here.

law.says: Section 147(1) applies to "any vehicle travelling upon a roadway at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place" and requires it, "where practicable", to be driven in the right-hand lane then available or as close as practicable to the right curb or edge.

flags.definition: A vehicle travelling at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place (147(1)).
flags.effect: Replace "slow traffic" with this, and add the Act's "where practicable".
flags.note: 147(3) makes it an offence (fine $150 to $1,000). The sign itself is a regulatory sign that must be obeyed (182(2)).

handbook.says: For the gap ahead only: the road test says to signal "when there is enough space for you to change lanes", to "keep at least a two- to three-second distance behind the vehicle in front of you" and not to "move in beside another vehicle or into the blind spot of another vehicle", while the gap behind is left at "no one is coming too fast from behind".

law.says: Section 148(2) makes turning out to the right for a faster overtaking vehicle a duty but sets no time, and 154(1)(a) allows the lane change only once the driver "first ascertains that it can be done safely".

flags.definition: At the first gap in the right-hand lane that lets the driver keep at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead without moving in beside another vehicle or into its blind spot.
flags.effect: Could replace "as soon as you can" with "at the first gap that meets the lane-change test".
flags.note: The gap behind ("no one is coming too fast from behind") and how long the driver may wait for a gap are not measured.

handbook.says: Its offence table lists "Failing to lower headlight beam" at two demerit points, the night-driving section repeats "Use your low-beam headlights ... when following a vehicle within 60 metres", and headlights are "required to be turned on" from half an hour before sunset to half an hour after sunrise and when people or vehicles less than 150 metres away cannot be clearly seen.

law.says: s. 168 (b) requires the driver of a motor vehicle with multiple-beam headlamps, on a highway at any time lighted lamps are required, to use the lower beam when "following another vehicle within 60 metres, except when in the act of overtaking and passing"; s. 62 (1) sets when lamps are required (half an hour before sunset to half an hour after sunrise, and whenever persons and vehicles are not clearly discernible at 150 metres or less), and O. Reg. 339/94 item 27 gives 2 demerit points.

flags.definition: A legal duty on any highway, divided or not: whenever lighted lamps are required (half an hour before sunset to half an hour after sunrise, or when persons and vehicles are not clearly discernible at 150 m), use the lower beam when following another vehicle within 60 m, except while overtaking and passing it.
flags.effect: Strength LAW, WHEN lighted lamps are required (s. 62 (1)); "all roads, including divided ones" matches "on a highway" in s. 168.
flags.note: Outside the times and conditions of s. 62 (1) the Act sets no beam duty, so there the rule stays advice. "These rules" also covers the 150 m oncoming-vehicle rule of 057.5, which is s. 168 (a).

handbook.says: The figures call 20 metres "the required stopping distance" for vehicles coming up behind a school bus with lights flashing, the same section says "You must obey the school bus law on any road", and the knowledge-test topics include "What drivers must do when they meet streetcars and school buses".

law.says: s. 175 (12.2) requires every driver approaching from the rear a stopped school bus that has its overhead red signal-lights flashing or its stop arm actuated to "stop at least 20 metres before reaching the bus", and s. 175 (17) makes contravening it an offence ($400 to $2,000 for a first offence).

flags.definition: A legal duty: when approaching from the rear a stopped school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm actuated, stop at least 20 m before reaching the bus.
flags.effect: Strength LAW; the condition covers red lights OR stop arm, and the 20 m is measured before reaching the bus.
flags.note: O. Reg. 339/94 item 14 gives 6 demerit points only for s. 175 (11) and (12), not (12.2), so the 20 m distance carries the s. 175 (17) fine but no listed demerit points.

handbook.says: It calls failing to stop "dangerous and illegal" and "illegal", says witnesses "can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus", and "You must obey the school bus law on any road", so going past the stopped bus is treated as law.

law.says: s. 175 (11), (11.1), (12) and (12.1) require the driver, whether meeting the bus on a highway without a median strip or approaching it from the rear, to stop and "not proceed until the bus moves or" the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing (red lights) or the stop arm is no longer actuated (stop arm); s. 175 (17) makes each an offence.

flags.definition: A legal duty: after stopping, do not proceed until the bus moves, or until the red lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is no longer actuated.
flags.effect: Strength LAW. The Act ends the wait when the bus moves OR the signals stop, so the statement's AND of all three conditions is stricter than the Act.
flags.note: Drivers meeting the bus on a highway with a median strip have no duty (s. 175 (11) and (11.1) exclude them).

handbook.says: It calls failing to stop "dangerous and illegal" and "illegal", says witnesses "can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus", and "You must obey the school bus law on any road", so going past the stopped bus is treated as law.

law.says: s. 175 (11) and (12) require the driver who meets, or approaches from the rear, a stopped school bus with its overhead red signal-lights flashing to stop and "not proceed until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing"; s. 175 (11.1) and (12.1) say the same for the stop arm, and s. 175 (17) makes each an offence.

flags.definition: A legal duty: after stopping for the bus, do not proceed until the bus moves or the overhead red lights have stopped flashing.
flags.effect: Strength LAW; the wording matches s. 175 (11) and (12).
flags.note: When the stop arm is also out, s. 175 (11.1) and (12.1) add: until the bus moves or the arm is no longer actuated. Meeting drivers on a highway with a median strip are excluded.

handbook.says: It calls failing to stop "dangerous and illegal" and "illegal", says witnesses "can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus", and "You must obey the school bus law on any road", so going past the stopped bus is treated as law.

law.says: s. 175 (11.1) and (12.1) require a driver stopped for a school bus with its stop arm actuated not to proceed "until the bus moves or the stop arm is no longer actuated", and s. 175 (11) and (12) say the same for the overhead red lights; s. 175 (17) makes each an offence.

flags.definition: A legal duty: stay stopped until the bus moves, or until the stop arm is no longer actuated and the red lights have stopped flashing.
flags.effect: Strength LAW; add that the duty also ends when the bus moves.

handbook.says: The regulatory-sign list says the two-way left-turn sign "means the lane is only for two-way left turns", and regulatory signs "give a direction that must be obeyed"; for an unsigned lane the handbook gives no legal marker.

law.says: Under O. Reg. 615 s. 34 (3) and (4) (b) the Figure 7 Lane Designation sign, erected directly over a two-way left turn lane, means the lane "shall be used by a vehicle for the purpose only of making a left turn", and s. 182 (2) and s. 154 (1) (c) make drivers obey it; without such a sign, s. 154 (1) (b) lets a driver on a three-lane highway use the centre lane to overtake where the roadway is clearly visible and the lane is clear.

flags.definition: A legal duty where the lane carries the two-way left-turn Lane Designation sign (Figure 7): the lane is for left turns only, so passing in it is unlawful.
flags.effect: Strength LAW WHEN the lane carries the two-way left-turn sign; otherwise keep ADVICE (on a three-lane highway without the sign the Act allows passing in the centre lane).
flags.note: The handbook says the sign may be "above the road or on the ground", while s. 34 (4) (b) requires the Figure 7 sign to be erected directly over the lane.

handbook.says: The paragraphs before it say "The centre lane of some roads is used as a two-way left-turn lane", which "lets left-turning vehicles from both directions wait", and "vehicles from the opposite direction also use this lane to turn left".

flags.definition: Two-way left-turn lanes: centre lanes used for left turns by traffic from both directions (Diagram 2-36).
flags.effect: None; the statement already names them.

handbook.says: The neighbouring sentences add only open advice: unnecessary lane changes make a collision more likely, "especially in heavy traffic or bad weather", and "If in doubt, do not pass"; nothing says when waiting is not safer.

flags.note: A description, not a duty; "heavy traffic or bad weather" names when changing lanes is riskier but does not bound "often".

handbook.says: It speaks of "Bicycles and mopeds travelling at a lower speed than other traffic", notes that cyclists may be "travelling at or faster than the normal speed of traffic", and tells turning drivers to "Slow down before you enter the turn", but never says when these road users are not slower.

flags.note: A description of traffic, not a duty; cyclists at or above the normal speed of traffic are one stated case where "usually" fails.

handbook.says: It narrows only by open conditions ("Never overtake and pass another vehicle unless you are sure you can do so without danger") and one exclusion ("Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions"); the slow-moving-vehicle sign list ("farm tractors, farm implements/machinery, and vehicles not capable of sustaining speeds over 40 km/h") names vehicles that carry the sign, not which ones a driver may want to pass.

flags.note: A description, not a duty. HTA s. 76 (2) defines "slow moving vehicles" for the sign, a narrower sense than the handbook's, and says nothing on which of them a driver may want to pass.

handbook.says: The snow-plow section warns "Do not try to pass between them" because it is "extremely dangerous", with no legal marker.

law.says: s. 148.1 (1) bans, only on a highway with a speed limit of 80 km/h or more that is divided into clearly marked lanes and only while travelling in a direction with two or more lanes, overtaking a snow plow "travelling in echelon with another plow or plows" unless the overtaking lane is entirely clear of any part of the plow, its attachments or blade.

flags.definition: A legal duty only for snow plows in echelon on highways posted 80 km/h or more with two or more marked lanes in the driver's direction, unless the overtaking lane is entirely clear of the plow and its blade.
flags.effect: Keep ADVICE for the general ban; the echelon case on such highways is LAW under s. 148.1 (1).
flags.note: s. 148.1 (2) sets a fine of $150 to $1,000; the handbook's "under any conditions" is much broader than the Act.

handbook.says: The same item begins "If the vehicle you are passing speeds up, do not race", and the sanctions section lists both "driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing" and "street racing" among dangerous behaviours, so either reading of the pronoun names conduct the handbook treats as sanctioned.

law.says: s. 148 (2) requires a driver being overtaken to "turn out to the right and allow the overtaking vehicle ... to pass"; s. 172 (1) bans driving in a race or contest or while performing a stunt, and O. Reg. 455/07 makes a stunt of "driving a motor vehicle in a manner that indicates an intention to prevent another vehicle from passing" (s. 3, para. 8 i) and a race of two or more vehicles driven at a marked departure from the lawful speed in competition (s. 2 (1), para. 1); no provision names speeding up as such.

flags.definition: Unlawful when the speeding up fails to allow the overtaking vehicle to pass (s. 148 (2)) or indicates an intention to prevent it from passing (a stunt under s. 172 (1) and O. Reg. 455/07, s. 3, para. 8 i); racing the passing vehicle at a marked departure from the lawful speed is a race under s. 172 (1).
flags.effect: Read "It" as the speeding up in 018.3, the nearest antecedent; racing is unlawful separately. Keep MUST NOT, citing s. 148 (2) and s. 172 (1).
flags.note: Speeding up that neither stops the pass nor shows an intent to prevent it is not clearly covered by any provision.

handbook.says: Elsewhere it says bicycles and mopeds "can use any part of the lane if necessary for safety, such as to" avoid "puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates", and that riders "may make sudden moves because of uneven road surfaces or poor weather conditions"; these are open examples, not a frequency.

flags.note: A description of riders, not a duty; the examples would let "often" read "when necessary for safety", but they stay open-ended ("such as").
