flags.effect: Replace "one of many high-speed roads with 3 or more lanes" with the scheduled portions, "truck" with a commercial motor vehicle (alone or towing) over 6.5 m long, and add the s. 1 (2) exceptions; where the left lane is an HOV lane, the barred lane is the one next to it.
flags.note: The regulation does not turn on the number of lanes or on "high-speed"; the handbook's "three or more lanes in each direction" is descriptive.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p6a|X|Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads

handbook.says: The rule is restated in agreeing advisory words for freeways (“Traffic should keep to the right, using the left lanes for passing”; “Drive in the right-hand lane when possible”; “Get into the habit of driving in the right lane, leaving the other lanes clear for passing”), and the sign caption “Slow traffic on multi-lane roads must keep right” makes it a “must” only for slow traffic.

law.says: No provision makes keeping right a duty for every driver: only a vehicle travelling “at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place” must keep to the right-hand lane or right edge “where practicable” (147 (1)), with exceptions “while overtaking and passing” and “while preparing for a left turn” (147 (2)), and a driver meeting another vehicle must “turn out to the right from the centre of the roadway” (148 (1)).

flags.definition: Keeping right is advice for every driver, except to turn left or to pass; it is a legal duty only for a vehicle travelling below the normal speed of traffic at that time and place, where practicable (147 (1), (2)), and for a driver meeting oncoming traffic (148 (1)).
flags.effect: None; p6a stays advice, the restatements agree with it, and the sign's "must" belongs to the slow-traffic duty.
flags.note: 147 (2) gives the same two exceptions as the handbook: overtaking and passing, and preparing for a left turn.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p6b|X|especially important if you are driving more slowly than other vehicles

handbook.says: The sign caption restates it as a duty, “Slow traffic on multi-lane roads must keep right”, where this paragraph gives it as advice that is especially important for slower drivers.

law.says: No provision makes keeping right a duty for every driver: a vehicle travelling “at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place shall, where practicable,” be driven in the right-hand lane or as close as practicable to the right edge (147 (1)), except “while overtaking and passing” or “while preparing for a left turn” (147 (2)), and a fine of $150 to $1,000 applies (147 (3)).

flags.definition: Driving more slowly than other vehicles = travelling at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place; such a driver must, where practicable, keep to the right-hand lane then available or as close as practicable to the right curb or edge, on any roadway, except while overtaking and passing or preparing for a left turn.
flags.effect: Strength becomes LAW (147 (1)), qualified by "where practicable" and the 147 (2) exceptions; the sign's multi-lane limit is narrower than the Act, which covers every roadway.
flags.note: O. Reg. 339/94 lists no demerit points for s. 147.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p11b|X|you should change lanes to pass

handbook.says: The passing section gives the same advice for “Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds” without the hedge (“Do not take this as an invitation to pass in the same lane”; “If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes”), while the cyclist section keeps the hedge whenever possible and also allows for passing within the lane (“Discourage passing where the lane is too narrow to be shared safely”; “When passing a cyclist, drivers of motor vehicles must maintain a minimum distance of one metre”).

law.says: The Act requires no lane change to pass a bicycle: the overtaking vehicle “shall turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision” (148 (6)) and must leave “a distance of not less than one metre”, “as nearly as may be practicable” (148 (6.1)), with 2 demerit points (O. Reg. 339/94, item 44).

flags.definition: Changing lanes to pass a cyclist is advice in both passages, not a legal duty; the law lets a driver pass a cyclist within the lane if at least one metre is left, which fits the cyclist section's "whenever possible" but not the passing section's unhedged wording.
flags.effect: None to strength (ADVICE stays); whether the advice is hedged by [?possible] stays open, because the two passages differ.

handbook.says: The handbook uses overtaking and passing for one act (“Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”; “After overtaking, ... the vehicle you are passing”), and the cyclist section itself says “When passing a cyclist” for the one-metre rule.

law.says: The Act says “overtaking a person travelling on a bicycle” and “until safely past the bicycle” (148 (6.1)), and uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) without defining any of them.

flags.definition: Overtaking a cyclist = passing the cyclist: moving past the cyclist from behind.
flags.effect: None; the statement already says passing.
flags.note: The handbook's "When passing a cyclist" sentence restates 148 (6.1), whose word is "overtaking".

handbook.says: The section introduces “large commercial vehicles such as tractor-trailers and buses” and goes on “sharing the road with large commercial vehicles means you must always be aware of a large vehicle’s capabilities”, so “large vehicle” is its short form for the same vehicles.

law.says: No provision uses "large vehicle" or "large commercial vehicle" or deals with cutting in front of one.

flags.definition: In this passage "large vehicle" is short for "large commercial vehicle", such as a tractor-trailer or a bus.
flags.effect: None; the statement says large vehicle.
flags.note: The Act defines "commercial motor vehicle" (s. 1 (1)) by body type with no size, so it does not fix "large"; the handbook gives examples only.

handbook.says: The two school-bus passages state the same duty with different names: “a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated” and “It is dangerous and illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its overhead red lights flashing” (Sharing the road) against “upper alternating red lights flashing” and “a stopped school bus that has its red lights flashing” (Stopping), while “overhead amber lights” are a separate warning.

law.says: The Act calls them “overhead red signal-lights” (175 (11), (12)) and says what they are: a school bus made on or after January 1, 2005 carries “four overhead red signal-lights” mounted “at or near the roof line”, one on each side at the front and at the rear (175 (4.1)); it does not say they alternate.

flags.definition: Overhead red lights, upper alternating red lights, red alternating lights and (in the Stopping note) red lights all name the bus's overhead red signal-lights: the red signal-lights at or near the roof line (175 (4.1)), not the amber ones.
flags.effect: None; the wordings name the same lights, and the Act's term is overhead red signal-lights.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p23a|X|You must stop whenever you approach a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing

handbook.says: The Sharing-the-road list states the duty for “a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated” (“You must stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus”), while the Stopping page states it for a bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing and for one “that has its red lights flashing” and mentions the stop sign arm only as something that “swings out after the upper alternating red lights begin to flash”.

law.says: The Act gives each signal its own duty to stop, for a stopped bus “that has its overhead red signal-lights flashing” (175 (11), (12)) or “that has its stop arm actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)), all punishable under 175 (17); O. Reg. 339/94 item 14 lists only “Subsections 175 (11) and (12)” for the 6 demerit points.

flags.definition: The duty to stop arises when the stopped bus has its overhead red signal-lights flashing or its stop arm actuated, either one alone, whether the driver meets it or comes from behind.
flags.effect: None; the statement names both signals, as the Act does; the Stopping page's wording without the stop arm is incomplete.
flags.note: By O. Reg. 339/94 item 14 the six demerit points attach to the red-light duties (175 (11), (12)); the stop-arm duties carry the 175 (17) fine but no listed demerit points.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p24a|X|only vehicles coming from behind the bus must stop

handbook.says: Both pages agree: “If you are on a roadway with a median strip, only vehicles approaching from the rear of the bus must stop” and “If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles coming from behind the bus must stop”, and the Stopping page explains “A median is a physical barrier such as a raised, lowered, earth or paved strip”.

law.says: The duty of a driver meeting the bus applies “on a highway, other than a highway with a median strip” (175 (11), (11.1)), while the duty when “approaching from the rear” applies on any highway (175 (12), (12.1)); “median strip” is defined in s. 1 (1).

flags.definition: On a highway with a median strip, a driver meeting the bus from the front need not stop; a driver approaching from the rear must stop on any highway.
flags.effect: None; both passages and the statement follow the Act.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p25a|X|If you are coming from behind the bus, stop at least 20 metres away.

handbook.says: The Sharing-the-road list gives the same distance, “If you are approaching from the rear of the vehicle, stop at least 20 meters away”, under a lead that covers a bus with “its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”; the Stopping page gives it for a bus with “its upper alternating red lights flashing”.

law.says: A driver “approaching from the rear a stopped school bus that has its overhead red signal-lights flashing, or that has its stop arm actuated, shall stop at least 20 metres before reaching the bus” (175 (12.2)).

flags.definition: From the rear, stop at least 20 m before reaching the bus when its overhead red signal-lights flash or its stop arm is actuated.
flags.effect: None; both passages give 20 m, as the Act does, and the statement names both signals.

handbook.says: The two school-bus passages give the same 20 m rule with different names for the lights: “a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated” (Sharing the road) and “a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing” (Stopping), which the Stopping page also calls “the upper alternating red flashing lights”.

law.says: The Act calls them “overhead red signal-lights” (175 (11), (12)) and says what they are: a school bus made on or after January 1, 2005 carries “four overhead red signal-lights” mounted “at or near the roof line”, one on each side at the front and at the rear (175 (4.1)); it does not say they alternate.

flags.definition: Overhead red lights, upper alternating red lights, red alternating lights and (in the Stopping note) red lights all name the bus's overhead red signal-lights: the red signal-lights at or near the roof line (175 (4.1)), not the amber ones.
flags.effect: None; both handbook wordings name the same lights.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p26a|X|until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated

handbook.says: The other passages give different end points: “Do not go until the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing” (either one ends it) and “Remain stopped until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing” (the bus moving is not mentioned), against this item's bus moving and lights stopped and arm no longer activated.

law.says: Each signal has its own end point: the red-light duty lasts “until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing” (175 (11), (12)) and the stop-arm duty “until the bus moves or the stop arm is no longer actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)).

flags.definition: A driver stopped for a school bus may go once the bus moves, or once every signal that was on has stopped: the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is no longer actuated.
flags.effect: Change UNTIL to: the school bus moves OR (the upper alternating red lights have stopped flashing AND the stop arm is no longer activated); as written the statement also waits for the bus to move after both signals are off.

handbook.says: The Stopping page states the same duty with “a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing” and “the upper alternating red flashing lights”, and the Sharing-the-road list's own lead says “overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”.

law.says: The Act calls them “overhead red signal-lights” (175 (11), (12)) and says what they are: a school bus made on or after January 1, 2005 carries “four overhead red signal-lights” mounted “at or near the roof line”, one on each side at the front and at the rear (175 (4.1)); it does not say they alternate.

flags.definition: Overhead red lights, upper alternating red lights, red alternating lights and (in the Stopping note) red lights all name the bus's overhead red signal-lights: the red signal-lights at or near the roof line (175 (4.1)), not the amber ones.
flags.effect: None; the handbook wordings name the same lights.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p28a|X|the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing

handbook.says: Other passages add the stop arm to the end point: “Do not proceed on your route until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated” and “Remain stopped until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing”.

law.says: Each signal has its own end point: the red-light duty lasts “until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing” (175 (11), (12)) and the stop-arm duty “until the bus moves or the stop arm is no longer actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)).

flags.definition: A driver stopped for a school bus may go once the bus moves, or once every signal that was on has stopped: the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is no longer actuated.
flags.effect: For the red lights alone the statement matches 175 (11) and (12); when the stop arm is also out, the driver must also wait until it is no longer actuated, unless the bus moves.

handbook.says: The paragraph goes on to call it “the arm” (“Remain stopped until the arm folds away”), and the Sharing-the-road list calls the same device “its stop arm” (“its stop arm activated”; “its stop arm is no longer activated”).

law.says: The Act uses “school bus stop arm” and “stop arm” for one device: the bus driver “shall actuate the school bus stop arm” and then “continue to operate the overhead signal-lights and stop arm” (175 (6)), and other drivers' duties turn on a bus “that has its stop arm actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)).

flags.definition: Stop sign arm = stop arm = the Act's school bus stop arm.
flags.effect: None; the statement says stop arm.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p33b|X|until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing

handbook.says: The other passages end the stop differently: “Do not go until the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing” and “Do not proceed on your route until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated”; only this sentence leaves out the bus moving.

law.says: Each signal has its own end point: the red-light duty lasts “until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing” (175 (11), (12)) and the stop-arm duty “until the bus moves or the stop arm is no longer actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)).

flags.definition: A driver stopped for a school bus may go once the bus moves, or once every signal that was on has stopped: the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is no longer actuated.
flags.effect: Add OR the school bus moves to UNTIL; the Act ends both duties once the bus moves.
flags.note: "All lights" includes the lights on the arm, which the Act covers by "the stop arm is no longer actuated".

flags.id: on-passing-1:p35a|X|Passing within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover is not permitted.

handbook.says: The Stopping page states the same ban: “You must not pass any vehicle within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover”.

law.says: When a vehicle “is approaching a pedestrian crossover and is within 30 metres of it”, a driver approaching from the rear “shall not allow the front extremity of his or her vehicle to pass beyond the front extremity of the other vehicle” (140 (3)), with 4 demerit points (O. Reg. 339/94, item 21).

flags.definition: Within 30 m of a pedestrian crossover, do not let the front of your vehicle pass beyond the front of another vehicle that is approaching the crossover.
flags.effect: None; both pages agree with each other and with 140 (3).

handbook.says: The next section defines “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle” and uses “Never overtake and pass another vehicle” and “If in doubt, do not pass” for the same act.

law.says: The Act uses the pair “overtaking and passing” (147 (2) (a), 150 (1), 154 (1) (b)) beside “overtake” (148 (2)) and “pass” (148 (8)) without defining any of them.

flags.definition: Overtaking and passing another vehicle = passing it: changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle.
flags.effect: None; the statement says pass.

handbook.says: The section defines “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”, and the passing steps say “After overtaking, ... the vehicle you are passing”, so changing lanes to overtake another vehicle is a pass.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: To overtake another vehicle = to pass it.
flags.effect: None; the statement says pass.

handbook.says: The next section defines “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”, which is going around the vehicle ahead, and the road test pairs the same moves (“leave enough space to pull out and pass”; “it lets you pull around the vehicle in front if it stalls”).

law.says: The Act says “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)), has no word for going around, and defines none of them.

flags.definition: Going around the vehicle ahead = passing it.
flags.effect: None; read it as passing.
flags.note: The vehicle here is one the driver is "behind", that is, following; going around a parked vehicle is named apart in 002.2.

handbook.says: The same paragraph ends “If in doubt, do not pass”, and the section opens “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”, so overtake and pass names the one act.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: Overtake and pass = pass.
flags.effect: None; the statement says pass.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p44b|X|Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions.

handbook.says: The winter section gives a narrower case of the same advice: on freeways “several snow plows may be staggered across the road” and “Do not try to pass between them”, which falls within the passing section's under any conditions; it also warns that “some snow plows have a wing that extends as far as three metres to the right”.

law.says: Only one case is law: on a highway with a speed limit of 80 km/h or more divided into clearly marked lanes, a driver travelling in a direction with two or more lanes may not “overtake a snow plow that is travelling in echelon with another plow or plows” unless the lane used “is entirely clear of any part of the snow plow, including any part of an attachment or the plow blade” (148.1 (1)).

flags.definition: Never passing a moving snow plow is advice; overtaking a plow in echelon on a highway with a speed limit of 80 km/h or more and two or more marked lanes in the driver's direction is an offence unless the lane used is entirely clear of every part of the plow, blade included (148.1 (1)).
flags.effect: Keep p44b as advice; the echelon case (p95d) is the part the Act makes law.
flags.note: The handbook's "staggered across the road" is the Act's "in echelon".

handbook.says: The section uses the words for one act: “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”, “Never overtake and pass another vehicle”, “If in doubt, do not pass”, and “You may pass on the right on multi-lane or one-way roads and when overtaking a streetcar or a left-turning vehicle”.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: After overtaking = after passing.
flags.effect: None; the procedure is for passing.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p49a|X|do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you

handbook.says: The sample test agrees: a driver about to be overtaken “must” “Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass” (key “5-d”), with “Speed up so that passing is not necessary” a wrong answer, and the licence page lists among “Other types of aggressive driving” “driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing”.

law.says: No provision names speeding up: a driver overtaken by a faster vehicle “shall turn out to the right and allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass” (148 (2), offence 148 (2.1)), and driving “in a manner that indicates an intention to prevent another vehicle from passing” is a stunt (O. Reg. 455/07, s. 3, para. 8 i), which 172 (1) prohibits.

flags.definition: Speeding up while being passed is unlawful where it keeps the other vehicle from passing (148 (2)) or shows an intention to prevent the pass (a stunt under 172 and O. Reg. 455/07, s. 3, para. 8 i); no provision forbids increasing speed as such.
flags.effect: Strength LAW holds for the cases 148 (2) and the stunt rule cover; for other speeding up the "unlawful" rests on the handbook alone.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p53c|X|If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes.

handbook.says: The cyclist section hedges the same advice, “Whenever possible, you should change lanes to pass”, and speaks of passing a cyclist within the lane (“must maintain a minimum distance of one metre”); for motorcycles it agrees (“Motorcycles use a full lane; treat them like other vehicles when driving”).

law.says: The Act requires no lane change: a vehicle overtaking a bicycle “shall turn out to the left so far as may be necessary to avoid a collision” (148 (6)) and leave “not less than one metre”, “as nearly as may be practicable” (148 (6.1)); it says nothing on lane changes for motorcycles or mopeds.

flags.definition: For motorcycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds the handbook agrees: pass by changing lanes. For bicycles both passages are advice, the law allows passing within the lane with at least one metre, and the cyclist section says "whenever possible", so the unhedged advice is not settled for bicycles.
flags.effect: None to strength (ADVICE); the hedge for bicycles stays open.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p54a|X|move to the right and let it pass in safety

handbook.says: The sample test says that when another vehicle “is about to overtake and pass your vehicle, you must” “Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass” (key “5-d”), and the same paragraph adds that on an undivided road the driver should “move closer to the right side of the lane”.

law.says: A driver “who is overtaken by a vehicle or equestrian travelling at a greater speed shall turn out to the right and allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass” (148 (2)); it is an offence (148 (2.1)) with 2 demerit points as “Failing to share road” (O. Reg. 339/94, item 22).

flags.definition: When overtaken by a faster vehicle, turn out to the right and let it pass; this is a legal duty.
flags.effect: Strength becomes LAW, as the test question says; "in safety" is not part of the Act's wording.
flags.note: The handbook's offence table lists "Failing to share the road" at two points, which O. Reg. 339/94 item 22 ties to 148 (2).

flags.id: on-passing-1:p55a|X|large trucks cannot travel in the far left lane

handbook.says: The Changing-positions page says “On many high-speed roads with three or more lanes in each direction, trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane” and “This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane”, against large trucks on many freeways on the Freeway page; neither names the roads or the size of truck.

law.says: O. Reg. 608, s. 1 (1) bars “a commercial motor vehicle or any combination of a commercial motor vehicle and a towed vehicle that exceeds 6.5 metres in length” from “the left lane” (or the lane next to a left-hand high occupancy vehicle lane) “of those portions of a highway described in the Schedules”, and s. 1 (2) exempts a bus, ambulance or fire apparatus, a vehicle engaged in maintenance or construction, a tow truck called to a vehicle in or near the left lane, and an emergency.

flags.definition: Trucks / large trucks = commercial motor vehicles, or combinations with a towed vehicle, over 6.5 m long, other than the exempt vehicles; the roads = the portions of Highways 400, 401, 403, 404, 407, 407 East, 409, 410, 417, 427, the QEW, the QEW/403 and Highways 7, 8 and 7/8 in Kitchener listed in the Schedules to O. Reg. 608.
flags.effect: Replace the [?many] high-speed roads (or freeways) with 3 or more lanes each way by the highway portions in the Schedules, and truck by a commercial motor vehicle or combination over 6.5 m; the regulation does not itself require three lanes.
flags.note: Where the left lane is an HOV lane, the barred lane is the one next to it.

handbook.says: The two passages describe the same ban and the same next lane: “large trucks cannot travel in the far left lane and must use the lane to the right for passing” and “This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane”.

law.says: The regulation calls it “the left lane” and, “where the left lane has been designated as a high occupancy vehicle lane”, bars “the lane adjacent to the high occupancy vehicle lane” instead (O. Reg. 608, s. 1 (1)).

flags.definition: Far left-hand lane = far left lane = the regulation's left lane (the leftmost lane in the driver's direction); next to a left-hand HOV lane, the barred lane is the one beside it.
flags.effect: None; the statement says far-left lane.

law.says: No provision names the inside or rear view mirror in passing; the Act only requires a mirror giving a view of the roadway to the rear.

flags.definition: Rear view mirror = inside (interior) mirror, the one that shows the rear window, not the side mirrors.
flags.effect: None; both procedures say inside mirror.
flags.note: Elsewhere the handbook says "rearview mirrors" in the plural (emergency-vehicle pages), where side mirrors may be meant; in the passing cue only the inside mirror fits.

law.says: The Act says “the right-hand lane then available for traffic” (147 (1)) and does not define it.

flags.effect: None; the statement says leftmost lane.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p73a|X|Traffic should keep to the right, using the left lanes for passing.

handbook.says: The same advice is given later on the Freeway page (“Use the far left lane of a multi-lane freeway to pass traffic moving slower than the speed limit, but don't stay there”; “Drive in the right-hand lane when possible”; “Get into the habit of driving in the right lane, leaving the other lanes clear for passing”) and for all roads (“Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle”).

law.says: No provision makes keeping right a duty for every driver: a vehicle travelling “at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place shall, where practicable,” be driven in the right-hand lane or as close as practicable to the right edge (147 (1)), except “while overtaking and passing” or “while preparing for a left turn” (147 (2)), and a fine of $150 to $1,000 applies (147 (3)).

flags.definition: Keeping right is advice for every freeway driver; it is a legal duty only for a vehicle travelling below the normal speed of traffic, where practicable, and not while overtaking and passing (147 (1), (2) (a)).
flags.effect: None; the statement stays advice, and the restatements agree.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p74c|X|must use the lane to the right for passing

handbook.says: The Changing-positions page says the same: “trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane” and “This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane”.

law.says: The regulation only bars such trucks from “the left lane” (or the lane next to a left-hand high occupancy vehicle lane) “of those portions of a highway described in the Schedules” (O. Reg. 608, s. 1 (1)); that they pass in the next lane follows from that ban.

flags.definition: A truck covered by O. Reg. 608 may not use the left lane of a scheduled highway portion, so its passing lane is the lane next to it.
flags.effect: None; both passages agree; the "must" reflects the ban on the left lane, not a separate duty.
flags.note: Where the left lane is an HOV lane, the barred lane is the one next to the HOV lane.

handbook.says: The sentence before says “Drive in the right-hand lane when possible” for the same lane, and the all-roads rule says “Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads”.

law.says: The Act says “the right-hand lane then available for traffic” (147 (1)) and does not define it.

flags.definition: Right lane = right-hand lane.
flags.effect: None; the statement says right-hand lane.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p77a|X|Check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic.

handbook.says: The list repeats it word for word, “Check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic”, right after “Wait for the emergency vehicle to pass”.

law.says: A driver stopped on the highway must, “before setting the vehicle in motion”, “first see that the movement can be made in safety” and give a signal if “the operation of any other vehicle may be affected” (142 (2)); moving from one lane to another carries the same duty (142 (1)).

flags.definition: Before merging back after pulling over for an emergency vehicle, check that the move can be made safely and signal; the Act requires both, the signal where other traffic may be affected.
flags.effect: None for the restatement; 142 (2) makes the check, and the signal where other traffic may be affected, a legal duty, so the strength could be LAW.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p77b|X|watch for other emergency vehicles that may be responding to the same call

handbook.says: The narrative gives the same advice: “Remain vigilant for additional emergency vehicles”.

law.says: No provision deals with watching for further emergency vehicles.

flags.definition: After an emergency vehicle has passed, watch for more emergency vehicles before moving on.
flags.effect: None; the passages agree.
flags.note: Each further emergency vehicle brings its own duty to pull over under 159 (1).

flags.id: on-passing-1:p81a|X|Failing to slow and carefully pass a stopped emergency vehicle

handbook.says: The narrative states the duty for “any emergency vehicle that is stopped with its red, or red and blue, lights flashing or a tow truck with its amber lights flashing”: “reduce the speed of your vehicle and proceed with caution”, while the offence table says slow and carefully pass and leaves out tow trucks.

law.says: The duty covers “an emergency vehicle with its lamp producing intermittent flashes of red light or red and blue light or a tow truck with its lamp producing intermittent flashes of amber light that is stopped on a highway”: the driver on the same side “shall slow down and proceed with caution” (159 (2), penalty 159 (6)), and O. Reg. 339/94 item 36.2 gives 3 points for “Failing to slow down and proceed with caution for emergency vehicle or tow truck”.

flags.definition: Slow down and proceed with caution when approaching, on the same side of the highway, a stopped emergency vehicle with red or red-and-blue lights flashing or a stopped tow truck with amber lights flashing.
flags.effect: None; the statement follows the Act; the offence table's wording is a shortened form.
flags.note: From January 1, 2027, 159 (2) also covers a stopped work-related vehicle with amber lights flashing.

handbook.says: The narrative gives the condition as “if safe to do so” (“you are required to move into a lane away from the emergency vehicle or tow truck, if safe to do so”; “When safe to do so, change lanes well in advance”), where the offence table says where possible.

law.says: On a highway with two or more lanes on that side, a driver in the stopped vehicle's lane or the lane next to it “shall move into another lane if the movement can be made safely” (159 (3)), and O. Reg. 339/94 names the offence “Failing to move into another lane for emergency vehicle or tow truck – if safe to do so” (item 36.3).

flags.definition: Move into another lane if the movement can be made safely; "where possible" in the offence table is a looser wording of the same condition.
flags.effect: Keep "if safe to do so"; the duty falls on a driver in the stopped vehicle's lane or the lane next to it, as 159 (3) says.
flags.note: From January 1, 2027, 159 (3) also covers stopped work-related vehicles.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p89a|X|Don't pass other vehicles or speed up suddenly.

handbook.says: The fog tips give the same advice twice more: “Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic” and “Don't speed up to pass a vehicle moving slowly”.

law.says: No provision deals with passing in fog.

flags.definition: In fog, do not pass.
flags.effect: None; the passages agree.

handbook.says: The whiteout tips repeat it, “Don't attempt to pass a vehicle moving slowly”, and the fog tips give the same advice, “Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic”.

law.says: No provision deals with passing in blowing snow or a whiteout.

flags.definition: In blowing snow or a whiteout, do not pass.
flags.effect: None; the passages agree.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p95d|X|Do not try to pass between them.

handbook.says: The passing section's “Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions” covers this case.

law.says: Only one case is law: on a highway with a speed limit of 80 km/h or more divided into clearly marked lanes, a driver travelling in a direction with two or more lanes may not “overtake a snow plow that is travelling in echelon with another plow or plows” unless the lane used “is entirely clear of any part of the snow plow, including any part of an attachment or the plow blade” (148.1 (1)).

flags.definition: Do not pass between plows staggered (in echelon) across a freeway; on a highway with a speed limit of 80 km/h or more and two or more marked lanes in the driver's direction it is an offence unless the lane used is entirely clear of every part of the plow, blade included (148.1 (1)).
flags.effect: Strength becomes LAW for the case 148.1 (1) covers.
flags.note: "Staggered across the road" is the Act's "in echelon"; the Act excepts a lane entirely clear of the plow.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p98a|X|Slow traffic on multi-lane roads must keep right.

handbook.says: The all-roads rule gives it as advice, “Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle”, “especially important if you are driving more slowly than other vehicles”.

law.says: No provision makes keeping right a duty for every driver: a vehicle travelling “at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place shall, where practicable,” be driven in the right-hand lane or as close as practicable to the right edge (147 (1)), except “while overtaking and passing” or “while preparing for a left turn” (147 (2)), and a fine of $150 to $1,000 applies (147 (3)).

flags.definition: Slow traffic = a vehicle travelling at less than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place; it must, where practicable, use the right-hand lane then available or keep as close as practicable to the right curb or edge, except while overtaking and passing or preparing for a left turn.
flags.effect: Strength LAW confirmed; add "where practicable" and the 147 (2) exceptions; the Act's duty is not limited to multi-lane roads.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p100a|X|Stop for school bus when signals are flashing.

handbook.says: The general duty does not depend on a sign: “You must stop whenever you approach a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing” and “You must obey the school bus law on any road, no matter how many lanes or what the speed limit”, and the Sharing-the-road list gives the trigger as “overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”.

law.says: The duties to stop apply on every highway, with no sign required, for a stopped bus with its “overhead red signal-lights flashing” or its “stop arm actuated” (175 (11), (11.1), (12), (12.1)), and the Act's bus lettering says “do not pass when signals flashing” on buses made before 2005 and “do not pass when red lights flashing” on later ones (175 (3.1)).

flags.definition: Signals = the bus's overhead red signal-lights (or its stop arm); the duty to stop applies whether or not the sign is posted.
flags.effect: Drop "a sign is posted" from the condition; read signals as the red signal-lights or the stop arm.
flags.note: Overhead amber lights call only for slowing and preparing to stop (sharing-road-other-road-users:072.1, 074.1).

handbook.says: The Stopping page defines it: “A median is a physical barrier such as a raised, lowered, earth or paved strip constructed to separate traffic travelling in different directions” and “Vehicles cannot cross over a median strip”.

law.says: S. 1 (1) defines “median strip” as the portion of a highway built to separate traffic in opposite directions “by a physical barrier or a raised or depressed paved or unpaved separation area that is not intended to allow crossing vehicular movement”, and 175 (11) uses it for the exception.

flags.definition: Centre median divider = median strip: a physical barrier or raised or depressed separation area between opposing traffic that is not meant to be crossed (s. 1 (1)).
flags.effect: None; use median strip.

handbook.says: The passing and climbing lanes passage uses “right-hand lane” for the same lane: “These lanes let slower vehicles move into the right-hand lane so that faster ones can pass safely in the left lane”.

law.says: The Act says “the right-hand lane then available for traffic” (147 (1)) and lets a lane be designated “for slowly moving traffic” by official signs (154 (1) (c)); neither defines it.

flags.definition: Right lane = right-hand lane: the lane on the right of the two-lane section.
flags.effect: None; the statement says right-hand lane.

handbook.says: The same lights are called “upper alternating red lights” (“You must stop whenever you approach a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing”; “The upper alternating red lights are not used for these stops”) and “overhead red lights” (“overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”).

law.says: The lights are the bus's “overhead red signal-lights”, four red lights mounted “at or near the roof line” (175 (4.1)); the bus driver's duty to “actuate the overhead signal-lights” and “the school bus stop arm” (175 (6)) does not apply in a designated school bus loading zone (175 (13)).

flags.definition: Overhead red lights, upper alternating red lights, red alternating lights and (in the Stopping note) red lights all name the bus's overhead red signal-lights: the red signal-lights at or near the roof line (175 (4.1)), not the amber ones.
flags.effect: None; the statement says upper alternating red lights.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p123a|X|driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing

handbook.says: The passing section says “And do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you” and “It is unlawful and dangerous”, and the sample test marks “Move to the left to prevent passing” wrong and “Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass” right (key “5-d”).

law.says: Driving without due care or consideration “by, i. driving a motor vehicle in a manner that indicates an intention to prevent another vehicle from passing” is a stunt (O. Reg. 455/07, s. 3, para. 8 i), which 172 (1) prohibits, and the overtaken driver must “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass” (148 (2)).

flags.definition: Driving in a manner that indicates an intention to prevent another vehicle from passing is a stunt, prohibited by s. 172.
flags.effect: None; the statement follows the regulation; the narrower "do not speed up" (p49a) is one way of doing it.
flags.note: O. Reg. 339/94 item 3 gives six demerit points for any s. 172 offence.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p130a|X|Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass.

handbook.says: The passing section gives the same move: “When faster traffic wants to pass you, move to the right and let it pass in safety”, and on an undivided road “move closer to the right side of the lane”.

law.says: A driver “who is overtaken by a vehicle or equestrian travelling at a greater speed shall turn out to the right and allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass” (148 (2)); it is an offence (148 (2.1)) with 2 demerit points as “Failing to share road” (O. Reg. 339/94, item 22).

flags.definition: When overtaken, turn out to the right and let the vehicle pass; this is a legal duty.
flags.effect: None; the statement already has strength LAW, which 148 (2) confirms; the advice in p54a should take the same strength.

handbook.says: The same question uses both words for one act: “Speed up so that passing is not necessary”, “Move to the left to prevent passing” and “Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass” answer a stem about a vehicle about to overtake and pass your vehicle.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: Overtake and pass = pass.
flags.effect: None; the statement says pass.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p131a|X|When stopped behind another vehicle at the intersection, leave enough space to pull out and pass without having to back up.

handbook.says: The turn task gives it in the same words (“When stopped behind another vehicle at an intersection, leave enough space to pull out and pass without having to back up”), and the business and residential tasks give a like rule, “leave enough space to see its rear wheels or to pull around it without having to back up”.

law.says: No provision deals with the space to leave behind a stopped vehicle.

flags.definition: When stopped behind another vehicle, leave enough space to pull out and around it without backing up.
flags.effect: None; the passages agree.
flags.note: The rear-wheels cue in the business and residential tasks is a checkable test the intersection tasks lack.

handbook.says: The handbook uses the words for one act: “Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle”, “Never overtake and pass another vehicle unless you are sure you can do so without danger to yourself or others”, “If in doubt, do not pass”, and “After overtaking, ... the vehicle you are passing”.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: Another vehicle overtaking you = another vehicle passing you.
flags.effect: None; the statement says pass.

handbook.says: The road test pairs the same moves (“leave enough space to pull out and pass”; “it lets you pull around the vehicle in front if it stalls”), and the passing section calls going past a left-turning vehicle a pass (“You may drive on the right shoulder only to pass a vehicle turning left”).

law.says: The Act calls going past a vehicle that “is making or about to make a left turn” on its right to “overtake and pass” it (150 (1)), has no word for going around, and defines none of them.

flags.definition: Pulling out to go around the vehicle = pulling out to pass it.
flags.effect: None; read it as passing.

handbook.says: The handbook uses overtaking and passing for one act (“You may pass on the right ... when overtaking a streetcar or a left-turning vehicle”; “After overtaking, ... the vehicle you are passing”) and calls a cyclist coming up beside a parked car “a passing cyclist”.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: Traffic or pedestrians overtaking you on the right = moving past you on the right from behind.
flags.effect: None; the statement says passing.
flags.note: For pedestrians and cyclists the word cannot mean the lane change in the handbook's definition of passing (012.1); it means moving past from behind.

handbook.says: The intersection tasks use both for one move: “leave enough space to pull out and pass without having to back up” and “it lets you pull around the vehicle in front if it stalls”.

law.says: The Act says “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)), has no word for pulling around, and defines none of them.

flags.definition: Pull around the stopped vehicle = pull out and pass it.
flags.effect: None; read it as passing.

flags.id: on-passing-1:p137a|X|leave enough space to see its rear wheels or to pull around it without having to back up

handbook.says: The residential task repeats it word for word (“When you stop behind another vehicle, leave enough space to see its rear wheels or to pull around it without having to back up”), and the intersection tasks give the same rule without the rear-wheels cue: “leave enough space to pull out and pass without having to back up”.

law.says: No provision deals with the space to leave behind a stopped vehicle.

flags.definition: When stopped behind another vehicle, leave enough space to see its rear wheels, or to pull out around it without backing up.
flags.effect: None; the passages agree.

handbook.says: The handbook uses the words for one act: “Changing your position on the road involves changing lanes or overtaking and passing another vehicle”, “Never overtake and pass another vehicle”, “If in doubt, do not pass”, “After overtaking, ... the vehicle you are passing”, and “pass on the right ... when overtaking a streetcar”.

law.says: The Act uses “overtake” (148 (2)), “pass” (148 (8)) and “overtake and pass” (150 (1)) for this act and defines none of them; 148 (2) has the overtaken driver “allow the overtaking vehicle or equestrian to pass”.

flags.definition: Passing = overtaking = overtaking and passing.
flags.effect: None; keep ALSO CALLED overtaking.
flags.note: The handbook also uses both words for moves without a lane change (passing a cyclist with a one-metre gap; pedestrians overtaking on the right), so its definition of passing as a lane change is narrower than its use of either word.

handbook.says: The night passing steps give the same cue with “rear view mirror” (“When you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror”), the road test names “your rearview and side mirrors” as different mirrors, and the set-up section calls it “the interior mirror”.

law.says: No provision names the inside or rear view mirror in passing.

flags.definition: Inside mirror = rear view mirror = interior mirror, the one that shows the rear window.
flags.effect: None; both procedures say inside mirror.

handbook.says: Both pages give the same ban: “Passing within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover is not permitted” and “You must not pass any vehicle within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover”.

law.says: When a vehicle “is approaching a pedestrian crossover and is within 30 metres of it”, a driver approaching from the rear “shall not allow the front extremity of his or her vehicle to pass beyond the front extremity of the other vehicle” (140 (3)), with 4 demerit points (O. Reg. 339/94, item 21).

flags.definition: Within 30 m of a pedestrian crossover, do not let the front of your vehicle pass beyond the front of another vehicle that is approaching the crossover.
flags.effect: None; both pages agree with each other and with 140 (3).

handbook.says: The day passing steps give the same cue with “when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror”, the road test names “your rearview and side mirrors” as different mirrors, and the set-up section calls it “the interior mirror”.

law.says: No provision names the inside or rear view mirror in passing.

flags.definition: Rear view mirror = inside (interior) mirror, the one that shows the rear window, not the side mirrors.
flags.effect: None; both procedures say inside mirror.

handbook.says: The pedestrians page gives the same advice, “Pass these safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed” and “Always be ready, in case pedestrians make sudden or unexpected moves”, for “a special safety island or zone for passengers”, which the streetcar page calls “an area has been set aside for streetcar passengers”.

law.says: No provision sets a speed for passing a streetcar safety island or zone.

flags.definition: Pass streetcar safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed and be ready for sudden moves by pedestrians.
flags.effect: None; the statement already joins both passages.
flags.note: 166 (1) names the place "a safety zone" set aside by by-law and lifts the 2 m stop rule there, but sets no speed for passing it.

handbook.says: The Sharing-the-road list makes the stop arm a trigger of its own (“When you see a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”; “You must stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus”; “It is dangerous and illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated”).

law.says: A stopped bus “that has its stop arm actuated” brings its own duty to stop, meeting it (175 (11.1)) or from the rear (175 (12.1)), beside the red-light duties (175 (11), (12)), all punishable under 175 (17); O. Reg. 339/94 item 14 lists only “Subsections 175 (11) and (12)” for the 6 demerit points.

flags.definition: Stop for a stopped school bus with its overhead red signal-lights flashing or with its stop arm actuated, either one alone.
flags.effect: Add OR its stop arm is actuated.
flags.note: By O. Reg. 339/94 item 14 the six demerit points attach to the red-light duties; the stop-arm duties carry the 175 (17) fine.

flags.id: mto:3.4.12d|X|and its stop arm is no longer activated

handbook.says: The other passages give different end points: “Do not proceed on your route until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated” and “Remain stopped until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing”.

law.says: Each signal has its own end point: the red-light duty lasts “until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing” (175 (11), (12)) and the stop-arm duty “until the bus moves or the stop arm is no longer actuated” (175 (11.1), (12.1)).

flags.definition: A driver stopped for a school bus may go once the bus moves, or once every signal that was on has stopped: the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is no longer actuated.
flags.effect: For the red lights alone the statement matches 175 (11) and (12); when the stop arm is also out, the driver must also wait until it is no longer actuated, unless the bus moves.
flags.note: Each signal is its own duty, each lasting until the bus moves or that signal stops.

handbook.says: The narrative gives the condition as “if safe to do so” (“you are required to move into a lane away from the emergency vehicle or tow truck, if safe to do so”; “When safe to do so, change lanes well in advance”), where the offence table says where possible.

law.says: On a highway with two or more lanes on that side, a driver in the stopped vehicle's lane or the lane next to it “shall move into another lane if the movement can be made safely” (159 (3)), and O. Reg. 339/94 names the offence “Failing to move into another lane for emergency vehicle or tow truck – if safe to do so” (item 36.3).

flags.definition: Move into another lane if the movement can be made safely; "where possible" in the offence table is a looser wording of the same condition.
flags.effect: Keep "if safe to do so"; the duty falls on a driver in the stopped vehicle's lane or the lane next to it, as 159 (3) says.
flags.note: From January 1, 2027, 159 (3) also covers stopped work-related vehicles.

handbook.says: The Changing-positions page says many high-speed roads where the Freeway page says many freeways: “On many high-speed roads with three or more lanes in each direction, trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane”; neither names the roads.

law.says: O. Reg. 608, s. 1 (1) bars “a commercial motor vehicle or any combination of a commercial motor vehicle and a towed vehicle that exceeds 6.5 metres in length” from “the left lane” (or the lane next to a left-hand high occupancy vehicle lane) “of those portions of a highway described in the Schedules”, and s. 1 (2) exempts a bus, ambulance or fire apparatus, a vehicle engaged in maintenance or construction, a tow truck called to a vehicle in or near the left lane, and an emergency.

flags.definition: Trucks / large trucks = commercial motor vehicles, or combinations with a towed vehicle, over 6.5 m long, other than the exempt vehicles; the roads = the portions of Highways 400, 401, 403, 404, 407, 407 East, 409, 410, 417, 427, the QEW, the QEW/403 and Highways 7, 8 and 7/8 in Kitchener listed in the Schedules to O. Reg. 608.
flags.effect: Replace the [?many] high-speed roads (or freeways) with 3 or more lanes each way by the highway portions in the Schedules, and truck by a commercial motor vehicle or combination over 6.5 m; the regulation does not itself require three lanes.
flags.note: Where the left lane is an HOV lane, the barred lane is the one next to it.

flags.id: mto:3.1.2a|G|on the left of a centreline

law.says: Section 149 (1) (a) also bans the means, not the pass: no vehicle may be driven "to the left of the centre of a roadway designed for one or more lanes of traffic in each direction" within 30 metres of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel where the view is obstructed, and 149 (2) (a) lifts it where there are more lanes in one direction than the other.

flags.definition: Driving left of the centre of a roadway with one or more lanes in each direction, within 30 m of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel where the view is obstructed (149 (1) (a)); a pass that stays right of the centre is not covered, in the Act either.
flags.effect: None; the gap is in the Act too, and a road with more lanes in one direction than the other is excepted (149 (2) (a)).
flags.note: The handbook mentions bridges and tunnels elsewhere only for U-turns and three-point turns, not for passing.

handbook.says: The handbook names the illegal act as not stopping: "It is illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its red lights flashing", "It is dangerous and illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated", and its offence table lists "Failing to stop for a school bus".

law.says: Section 175 (11) and (12) require a driver meeting or coming up behind a stopped school bus with its overhead red lights flashing to stop and "not proceed until the bus moves or the overhead red signal-lights have stopped flashing"; (11.1) and (12.1) say the same for the stop arm. There is no separate ban on passing.

flags.definition: Failed to stop for a stopped school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm out, or went on before the bus moved or the signals stopped (175 (11) to (12.1)).
flags.effect: Read "illegally passed" as "failed to stop for".
